title: Rules That Protect Participants
objective: After this level you can explain informed consent and ethics review boards, and the studies that made them necessary.
summary: Abuses like Nazi experiments and the Tuskegee syphilis study led to consent rules and ethics review boards. Today participants must know the risks and can quit anytime.

cards.headline: Before a study on people starts, a committee has to say yes.
cards.body: In the United States, a review board generally has to approve research on people before it begins. That wasn't always so. The rules exist because of studies that did serious harm to people who never agreed to it.

events.label: The US Public Health Service starts a syphilis study in Alabama without consent
Nuremberg Code, after Nazi doctors' trial: voluntary consent is essential
Press reports end the Tuskegee study
National Research Act passes in response
Belmont Report: respect for persons, beneficence, justice

cards.headline: The Tuskegee study
cards.body: In 1932 the US Public Health Service began studying syphilis in 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 with the disease and 201 without. Their informed consent was never collected. The men with syphilis were not told they had it, and when penicillin became an effective treatment in the 1940s, they were not given it. The study ran until 1972, when the press exposed it. The outrage led directly to the National Research Act of 1974.

cards.headline: What protection looks like today
cards.body: Now an institutional review board, a committee of scientists, administrators and community members, reviews a study before it can proceed. Participants give informed consent: they learn what to expect, including risks, and know they can quit at any time without penalty, with their data kept confidential. Parents sign for anyone under 18. If a study used deception, everyone gets a full, honest debriefing at the end. It's also why some questions, like swapping babies between families, stay off-limits.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: consent means knowing the risks, choosing freely and being free to stop.

cards.headline: Protecting people
learned: Tuskegee's exposure led to the 1974 National Research Act
Consent: know the risks, choose freely, quit anytime

questions.prompt: Under informed consent, what can a participant do partway through a study?

options.label: Nothing: consent is binding until the end
Quit at any time without penalty
Quit only with the review board's permission
options.rationale: No permission is needed to stop.

options.label: Quit only if their data are deleted first
options.rationale: Stopping doesn't depend on any condition.

questions.explanation: Informed consent makes clear that taking part is voluntary and can be stopped at any time without penalty.

questions.prompt: How did the Tuskegee syphilis study lead to new US research rules?

options.label: Its exposure in 1972 caused outrage that led to the National Research Act
Its researchers asked Congress for stricter rules
options.rationale: The study ended because the press exposed it, not at the researchers' request.

options.label: It proved that penicillin did not work
options.rationale: Penicillin worked; the men were denied it.

options.label: It was the first study to use consent forms
options.rationale: The men's consent was never collected.

questions.explanation: The press exposed the study in 1972, and the outrage led directly to the National Research Act of 1974.

questions.prompt: Level 7 relied on twins and adoptees instead of assigning children to families. Which body would stop a plan to assign them today?

options.label: A licensure exam board
options.rationale: That board licenses psychologists; it doesn't review studies.

options.label: The APA's 54 divisions
options.rationale: Divisions are interest groups, not review committees.

questions.explanation: An institutional review board reviews proposals for research with people, and ethics rule out many such experiments.
